docs.title: Isolating Sensor Faults from Mechanical Events in Robot Joint Actuators
docs.text:
A model-based fault detection and isolation scheme for PMSM robot joint actuators that tells sensor faults apart from collisions and payload changes, using only signals the FOC loop already computes.

Lakshanand Sugumar · Arizona State University · Work-in-progress draft (simulation results; hardware validation in progress)

PMSMFOCFault detection & isolationMomentum observerBack-EMF residual

Read the method PDF draft

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text: A joint actuator that stops on every anomaly is safe but unusable, and one that ignores anomalies is dangerous; the right reaction depends on whether the fault is in the sensor or in the mechanics. We present a model-based fault detection and isolation (FDI) scheme for permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) joint actuators that separates the two classes using only signals the field-oriented control (FOC) loop already computes. A back-EMF voltage residual, built from the commanded dq voltages, measured currents, and encoder speed, responds to encoder faults but is structurally insensitive to load torque. A generalized-momentum observer responds to external torque but is trusted only while the voltage residual certifies the encoder. Together with a short angle-free voltage-pulse test, the residuals isolate encoder faults, phase open circuits, collisions, and load changes, and select a class-specific reaction. In a simulation study with model errors of up to \SI{30}{\percent}, 300 Monte Carlo fault trials, and one hour of normal motion, the scheme isolated 299 of 300 faults with no false alarms. Encoder faults raised an alarm within \SI{0.51}{\milli\second} and were isolated in a median of \SI{3.5}{\milli\second}; collisions were detected in a median of \SI{2.3}{\milli\second} against \SI{7.0}{\milli\second} for a following-error check, which also raised false alarms in \SI{22}{\percent} of normal runs. \TBD{One sentence on hardware results.}

docs.title: The idea in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  F[FOC loop signals: commanded dq voltages, measured currents, encoder speed] --> RV[Back-EMF voltage residual r_v]
  F --> RM[Generalized-momentum observer r_m]
  RV -->|fires| ENC[Encoder fault → safe state]
  RV -->|quiet: encoder certified| TRUST[Trust r_m]
  TRUST --> RM
  RM -->|fires| MECH[Mechanical event]
  MECH --> PT[Short angle-free voltage-pulse test]
  PT --> C1[Collision → reflex]
  PT --> C2[Load change → adapt]
  PT --> C3[Phase open → safe state]

The back-EMF residual responds to encoder faults but is structurally insensitive to load torque. The momentum observer responds to external torque, but is trusted only while the voltage residual certifies the encoder. A joint that stops on every anomaly is safe but unusable; this scheme lets it pick a reaction that fits the fault.

docs.title: Discussion and Limitations
docs.text:
• Low speed. The encoder-fault signature scales with speed, so a frozen encoder is invisible to \(r_v\) below about 0.5 rad s−1 at the joint for these parameters. High-frequency injection could cover standstill at the cost of noise and losses.

  • Model error. Dead-time distortion, \(\lambda_m\) error, and thermal drift of \(R\) set \(\tau_v\); the thresholds tolerated about 1.5 times the assumed error bounds. Online \(R\) estimation would lower \(c_2\).

  • Collision reaction. The impact peak is set by the reflected inertia, so detection speed mainly prevents clamping rather than the first impact peak. The reflex also releases a payload for \(T_\mathrm{coll}\) before it is recognized as Load; for a leg in stance this would need a gentler first reaction (e.g. admittance) instead of zero torque.

  • Friction. Friction model error appears directly in \(r_m\) and sets the smallest detectable contact torque; a learned friction and cogging model would tighten this threshold.

  • Reaction to encoder faults. This paper stops at isolation and a safe state (ASC). Keeping the joint alive through sensorless control after an Enc alarm is ongoing work.

  • Simulation fidelity. The plant ignores cogging, magnetic saturation, gearbox backlash, and compliance, which hardware will add.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Two residuals already computable inside a PMSM joint actuator’s FOC loop, a back-EMF voltage residual and a generalized-momentum observer, have complementary sensitivity that isolates encoder faults from mechanical events without extra sensors. In simulation with up to 30 % model error, the scheme isolated 299 of 300 injected faults, raised no false alarms in an hour of normal motion, detected encoder faults within 0.51 ms, and detected collisions about three times faster than a following-error check. Future work extends the scheme to encoder-fault-tolerant control so that a humanoid joint can keep operating after a sensor fault.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Legged and humanoid robots are built from compact, highly geared or quasi-direct-drive joint actuators that run FOC at tens of kilohertz. Each actuator is a single point of failure: if the knee of a humanoid stops producing torque, the robot falls. At the same time, these actuators interact physically with people and the environment, so contacts must be detected fast enough to bound the contact force.

Most drives handle both problems with a small set of generic checks: hardware encoder error flags, over-current trips, and a following-error limit on \(|q_\mathrm{ref}-\hat q|\). These checks have two weaknesses. First, they are slow or blind for an important class of faults: an encoder that freezes or slips (for example, a shifted magnet, a stuck SPI read, or a corrupted but CRC-valid frame) raises no flag at all. Second, they do not isolate: a large following error can be caused by a collision, by a heavy payload, or by a wrong encoder angle that misaligns the current vector. These events call for opposite reactions. A collision calls for compliance, a payload change calls for compensating the load, and an encoder fault calls for leaving angle-dependent control, because any reaction that trusts the encoder will make things worse.

This paper asks whether a joint actuator can tell a sensor fault from a mechanical event using only signals the FOC loop already has, without additional sensors. Our answer is a pair of residuals with complementary sensitivity:

  • a back-EMF voltage residual \(r_v\) that compares the commanded \(dq\) voltages with those predicted by the electrical model at the encoder-reported speed and angle. Load torque changes the current, but the model accounts for the current, so \(r_v\) is insensitive to load; an encoder error changes the predicted back-EMF, so \(r_v\) is sensitive to encoder faults.

  • a generalized-momentum observer \(r_m\) that estimates the external joint torque. It responds to collisions and payload changes. It also reacts to encoder faults, because it uses the encoder speed, so its output is interpreted only while \(r_v\) is quiet.

Contributions. (i) A structured residual design for PMSM joint actuators that decouples encoder faults from external torque using only FOC signals (4); (ii) a decision logic, including an angle-free voltage-pulse test, that isolates four fault classes and maps each to a reaction (5); (iii) a simulation study with model error, Monte Carlo fault injection, long normal runs, and ROC analysis against a following-error baseline (6); and (iv) a hardware validation on with injected encoder faults, phase open circuits, and collisions at several speeds (7).

docs.title: Related Work
docs.text:
Model-based FDI. Residual generation with structured sensitivity is a classical tool for isolation. Our contribution is not a new observer class but a residual pair whose structural decoupling follows from the physics of the PMSM and joint, chosen so that it fits in the existing FOC interrupt.

Collision detection in robots. The generalized-momentum observer of De Luca et al. is the standard sensorless approach for manipulators and is surveyed in. These works assume healthy joint position sensing; we add a residual that certifies this assumption at run time.

Position sensor faults in PMSM drives. Sensor fault detection and tolerant control for electric drives has been studied mostly for traction and industrial drives, often by comparing the encoder with a sensorless estimate based on back-EMF. Open-phase faults and fault-tolerant topologies are reviewed in.

docs.title: Electrical model
docs.text: In the rotor reference frame, a surface PMSM obeys $\(\begin{aligned} v_d &= R\,i_d + L_d\,\dot i_d - \omega_e L_q\, i_q, \label{eq:vd}\\ v_q &= R\,i_q + L_q\,\dot i_q + \omega_e\,(L_d\, i_d + \lambda_m), \label{eq:vq} \end{aligned}\)$ where \(R\) is the phase resistance, \(L_{d,q}\) the inductances, \(\lambda_m\) the permanent-magnet flux linkage, and \(\omega_e = p\,\dot\theta_m\) the electrical speed for \(p\) pole pairs. The FOC loop computes the \(dq\) quantities with the measured electrical angle \(\hat\theta_e = p\,\hat\theta_m\). We write \(\delta = \theta_e - \hat\theta_e\) for the angle error and \(\hat\omega_e\) for the speed derived from the encoder.

docs.title: Mechanical model
docs.text: With gear ratio \(N\), torque constant \(k_t = \tfrac{3}{2}p\lambda_m\), and reflected inertia \(J\), the joint obeys $\(J\,\ddot q = \tau_m - \tau_f(\dot q) - \tau_g(q) + \tau_\mathrm{ext}, \qquad \tau_m = N k_t\, i_q, \label{eq:mech}\)$ where \(\tau_f\) is friction, \(\tau_g\) a known gravity or spring term (zero for a horizontal joint), and \(\tau_\mathrm{ext}\) the unknown external torque from contact or payload.

docs.title: Fault classes
docs.text: We consider four classes, summarized in 1: Enc (encoder freeze, offset/slip, or disconnect), Phase (open circuit of one motor phase), Coll (transient external torque from contact), and Load (persistent change in external torque, e.g. a payload).

docs.title: Back-EMF voltage residual
docs.text:
Let \(v^*_{dq}\) be the voltages commanded by the current controllers (available in the FOC loop before modulation). The model-predicted voltage at the encoder speed is $\(\hat v_{dq} = R\,i_{dq} + L\,\dot i_{dq} + \hat\omega_e \begin{bmatrix} -L_q i_q \\ L_d i_d + \lambda_m \end{bmatrix},\)$ and the residual is \(r_v = v^*_{dq} - \hat v_{dq}\). Neglecting inverter nonlinearity and parameter error for the moment, and expressing the true back-EMF in the frame defined by \(\hat\theta_e\), gives $\(r_v \approx \lambda_m \begin{bmatrix} -\omega_e \sin\delta \\ \omega_e\cos\delta - \hat\omega_e \end{bmatrix}. \label{eq:rv}\)$ Two properties follow directly from [eq:rv]:

  1. Load insensitivity. \(\tau_\mathrm{ext}\) enters only through \(i_{dq}\), which is measured and compensated in \(\hat v_{dq}\). Hence \(r_v \approx 0\) for any load when \(\delta = 0\) and \(\hat\omega_e = \omega_e\).

  2. Encoder sensitivity. An angle offset (\(\delta\ne0\)) gives \(\|r_v\|\approx 2\lambda_m|\omega_e\sin(\delta/2)|\), and a frozen encoder (\(\hat\omega_e \to 0\), \(\delta\) growing) gives \(\|r_v\|\approx\lambda_m|\omega_e|\).

To avoid differentiating noisy currents, \(r_v\) is computed after a first-order low-pass filter \(F(s)=a/(s+a)\) applied to both \(v^*\) and the model, with the \(L\,\dot i\) term computed as \(L\,a\,(i - F i)\). Unmodeled terms, mainly dead-time voltage error, thermal drift of \(R\), and error in \(\lambda_m\), are bounded by a threshold that follows their structure: $\(\|r_v\| > \tau_v = c_0 + c_1|\hat\omega_e| + c_2\|i_{dq}\|. \label{eq:thr_v}\)$ We set \(c_1 = 1.5\,\Delta\lambda_m\) and \(c_2 = 1.5\,\Delta R\) from the assumed parameter-error bounds, and \(c_0\) to 1.25 times the largest remaining residual over a calibration set of normal motion (6). Because the fault signature scales with \(|\omega_e|\), a frozen encoder is detectable only above \(|\omega_e| > c_0/(\lambda_m - c_1)\). A frozen reading at standstill is correct until the joint moves, so this limit mostly delays detection until motion starts (6).

docs.title: Generalized-momentum observer
docs.text:
Following, define the momentum \(\rho = J\dot q\) and the residual $\(r_m(t) = K\!\left[\rho(t) - \!\int_0^t\!\big(\tau_m - \hat\tau_f(\dot q) - \tau_g(q) + r_m\big)\,ds - \rho(0)\right], \label{eq:mo}\)$ with gain \(K>0\). Substituting [eq:mech] gives \(\dot r_m = K(\tau_\mathrm{ext} - r_m)\), so \(r_m\) is a first-order filtered estimate of \(\tau_\mathrm{ext}\) (plus friction and inertia model error) with bandwidth \(K\), and needs no acceleration measurement. An alarm is raised when \(|r_m| > \tau_m^\mathrm{thr}\).

The observer uses \(\dot q\) from the encoder, so an encoder fault corrupts \(r_m\): a freeze makes \(\rho\) drop to zero and \(r_m\) shows a spurious torque. In simulation \(r_m\) often alarms before \(r_v\) on an encoder freeze (2). This is why \(r_m\) alone cannot isolate, and why the logic below waits briefly for \(r_v\) before acting on a mechanical label.

docs.title: Discrete implementation
docs.text: Both residuals run at the current-loop rate \(f_s=20\) and need roughly 30 multiply-accumulates per cycle on top of FOC (our estimate). Each alarm requires \(n_d = 5\) consecutive samples (0.25 ms) over threshold.

docs.title: Fault Isolation and Reaction
docs.text:
is the structure (incidence) matrix of the residual set, extended with the reaction for each class.

Class \(r_v\) \(r_m\) pulse test Reaction Enc \(\ast\) balanced ASC Phase \(\ast\) one phase dead ASC Coll 0 transient – zero torque Load 0 persistent – resume + feedforward

Fault signatures and reactions.: residual fires; 0: residual stays below threshold; \(\ast\): may fire but is not trusted.

The logic is evaluated every cycle:

  1. \(r_v\) alarm. The encoder or the electrical path is suspect, so \(r_m\) is disregarded and the inverter enters active short circuit (ASC), a standard safe state for PMSM drives that needs no rotor angle. After 2 ms of settling, three 0.1 ms, 2 V voltage pulses are applied along the \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) phase axes in the stationary frame, again without the rotor angle. If one phase’s current response is below 30 % of the median response, the class is Phase; otherwise it is Enc.

  2. \(r_m\) alarm, \(r_v\) quiet. The event is treated as a possible collision at once: the torque command is set to zero (compliant). If \(r_v\) alarms within the next 40 ms, step 1 takes over. After \(T_\mathrm{coll}=40\) the class is Load if \(|r_m|\) is still above threshold, and position control resumes with \(-r_m\) as torque feedforward; otherwise the class is Coll and the joint stays compliant.

  3. Otherwise the actuator is healthy.

Reacting on the first \(r_m\) alarm keeps the collision reaction latency equal to the detection latency, at the cost of briefly releasing a payload before it is recognized as Load.

FDI architecture. Both residuals use only signals already present in the FOC loop; no sensors are added.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
The simulation models a small quasi-direct-drive actuator (2): a surface PMSM in the stationary frame integrated at 100 kHz; a three-phase inverter with 0.1 V dead-time voltage error; a 14-bit motor-side encoder; current-sensor noise of 30 mA rms; viscous and Coulomb friction; FOC at 20 kHz with 1.5 kHz current loops; and a 10 Hz PD position loop with model feedforward, all driven by the measured encoder angle. The speed estimate is a filtered encoder difference (300 Hz). Contacts are a spring-damper obstacle (100 N m rad−1). The controller and the residuals use a model whose parameters differ from the plant by uniform random errors of up to \(\pm20\) on \(R\), \(\pm5\) on \(\lambda_m\), \(\pm10\) on \(J\) and \(L\), and \(\pm30\) on both friction coefficients, drawn anew for every run. The parameters are representative values, not identified from our testbed.

Thresholds were calibrated once on 3 minutes of normal motion (sine, chirp to 4.5 Hz, and random minimum-jerk moves up to 6 rad s−1) and then frozen: \(c_0=0.23\), \(c_1=4.5e-4\), \(c_2=0.09\), \(\tau_m^\mathrm{thr}=0.093\). The baseline following-error check was calibrated the same way (1.25 times the largest value seen), giving 6.2 mrad.

Parameter Symbol Value Pole pairs \(p\) 14 Phase resistance \(R\) 0.30 Ω \(d\)/\(q\) inductance \(L_d=L_q\) 100 μH Flux linkage \(\lambda_m\) 6.0 mWb Gear ratio \(N\) 6 Joint-side inertia \(J\) 2.0 × 10−3 kg m2 Viscous / Coulomb friction \(b\), \(\tau_c\) 0.01 N m s rad−1, 0.05 N m Bus voltage / current limit – 24 V, 8 A Current-loop rate \(f_s\) 20 kHz Encoder resolution – 14 bit (motor side) Observer gain \(K\) 200  s Residual filter \(a\) \(2\pi\cdot500\)

docs.title: Silent encoder freeze
docs.text:
At \(t=0\) the encoder output is held at its last value with no error flag while the joint cruises at 1 rad s−1 (2). The angle error \(\delta\) grows with the true motion and \(r_v\) crosses its threshold after 0.60 ms. The momentum residual alarms even earlier, at 0.30 ms, because the speed estimate collapses; acting on it alone would mislabel the fault as a collision. The following-error check alarms only after 6.4 ms, and it cannot say whether the sensor or the mechanics failed.

Simulated silent encoder freeze at 1 rad s−1. Top: electrical angle error. Middle: back-EMF residual and its threshold. Bottom: momentum residual and threshold. Dotted lines mark alarms.

docs.title: Collision
docs.text:
shows an impact at 2 rad s−1. The momentum observer detects the contact 2.8 ms after impact, against 7.9 ms for the following-error check. With the proposed reaction the peak contact torque is 0.83 N m against 0.92 N m with the baseline; without any reaction the position controller keeps pushing and the contact torque rises to the current limit (6.1 N m) within 0.4 s. Throughout the collision \(\|r_v\|\) stays well below \(\tau_v\), confirming the load insensitivity predicted by [eq:rv].

Simulated collision at 2 rad s−1. Top: contact torque with no reaction, the following-error check, and the proposed observer. Middle: momentum residual. Bottom: back-EMF residual, which stays below its threshold.

docs.title: Effect of speed
docs.text:
sweeps the joint speed. Encoder-freeze detection by \(r_v\) takes 2.95 ms at 0.25 rad s−1 and 0.40 ms at 4 rad s−1, against 25.7 ms–1.7 ms for the following-error check. The analytic limit \(|\omega_e| > c_0/(\lambda_m-c_1)\) corresponds to 0.50 rad s−1 at the joint; the freeze at 0.25 rad s−1 is still caught because the position loop, seeing no motion, accelerates the joint past that limit. Collision detection takes 12.0 ms–2.0 ms with \(r_m\) and 30.5 ms–6.0 ms with the following error over the same range. The peak contact torque is dominated by the reflected inertia at impact, so faster detection lowers it only by 2 %–10 %; the main benefit of either reaction is to prevent the controller from clamping against the obstacle.

Speed sweep. Left: encoder-freeze detection latency (log scale). Right: peak contact torque in a collision.

docs.title: Monte Carlo isolation and false alarms
docs.text:
For each fault class we ran 50 trials with random model error, cruise speed \(|\dot q|\in[0.5,4]\,\), and fault time; encoder offsets were drawn from 20 °–90 ° electrical and load steps from 0.2 N m–0.8 N m. Separately, 180 held-out normal runs of 20 s each (one hour in total) measured false alarms. summarizes the results.

Fault Alarm Class Correct Foll. error Encoder freeze 0.27 (0.43) 3.5 (4.3) 49/50 3.1 (9.5) Encoder offset 0.22 (0.25) 3.2 (3.2) 50/50 0.22\(^a\) (41/50) Encoder unplug 0.23 (0.25) 3.2 (3.2) 50/50 0.23\(^a\) Phase open 1.3 (6.9) 4.2 (9.8) 50/50 67\(^b\) (41/50) Collision 2.3 (4.7) 42 (45) 50/50 7.0 (10.9) Load step 1.8 (3.7) 42 (44) 50/50 8.1 (14.4)

\(^a\)the measured position jumps, so the following error reacts at once but cannot tell a sensor jump from a real one. \(^b\)the position loop masks the lost torque for a long time.

Encoder faults were always detected within 0.51 ms, and collisions within 5.9 ms. The only misclassification was an encoder freeze at 0.51 rad s−1: \(r_m\) alarmed first, the collision reflex removed the torque, the joint coasted to a stop below the speed at which \(r_v\) can see the fault, and the event was labelled Coll. The reaction was still safe (zero torque), but the label was wrong; a check of \(r_v\) when control resumes, or the pulse test, would catch it. Neither residual raised a false alarm in the held-out hour, while the following-error check, calibrated the same way, alarmed in 22 % of the normal runs; its latency figures are therefore optimistic.

ROC. Sweeping a common multiplier on each threshold, with positives counted as detection within 20 ms and negatives as 1-second windows of normal motion, gives an area under the curve of 0.9999 for \(r_v\) on encoder faults (0.998 for the following error) and 0.9999 for \(r_m\) on collisions (0.9996). At the calibrated operating point \(r_v\) and \(r_m\) reach 100 % true positives with no false positives, whereas the following-error check reaches 94 % on encoder faults at a 1.2 % false-positive rate.

Robustness. Scaling all model-error bounds by 1.5 caused no false alarms in 30 runs; scaling by 2 caused \(r_m\) false alarms in 3 of 30 runs, and by 3 caused \(r_v\) false alarms in 3 and \(r_m\) in 5 of 30 runs. The thresholds therefore hold up to about 1.5 times the assumed parameter uncertainty, which sets how carefully \(\lambda_m\), \(R\), \(J\), and friction must be identified on hardware.
